analysis.one_liner: Lets unions require workers who benefit from contracts to pay dues, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2020 and referred to a Senate committee, which took no action before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law lets workers decline to join or financially support a union that represents them, and roughly half of states have added their own stronger 'right-to-work' laws. This bill would repeal the part of the National Labor Relations Act that allows those state laws, so in every state unions could require employees covered by a union contract to join or pay fees to the union that negotiates for them. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in unions, and workers in right-to-work states who could join or form stronger unions. Unions gain members and dues income, which supports higher bargaining budgets, and research generally finds unions raise wages for the workers they represent.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Union-represented workers, especially in right-to-work states

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that lets states ban union-security agreements requiring membership as a condition of employment [S3].

By preempting state right-to-work laws nationwide, it would allow unions in every state to collect dues from all employees covered by a union contract, giving unions more members and resources for negotiating pay and conditions [S2].
Seventeen senators — 16 Democrats and 1 Independent — sponsored or cosponsored the bill [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Some workers who would be required to join a union or pay dues or fees as a condition of keeping their job, even if they do not want to belong. Employers also face unions with stronger funding and fuller membership.
analysis.who_pays_short: Non-union workers and employers who pay higher dues

drawbacks.text: The bill forces workers who decline to join a union — for personal, political, or religious reasons — to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment, overriding state laws roughly half the states have chosen for themselves [S2].
Repealing Section 14(b) would override the policy choices of state legislatures and voters in right-to-work states, replacing them with a single federal rule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: requiring everyone covered by a union contract to contribute funds unions and strengthens their bargaining power, which tends to raise wages for represented workers. The cost falls on dissenting workers who must pay anyway, and on states that lose the right to set their own rule. The bill addressed the trade-off in one direction only — it made no provision for opting out or for agency-fee-only contributions — which is a fair criticism even from people who support union rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and that committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 5, 2020, and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote — before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].
All 17 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Business and employer groups opposed to union security requirements, and non-union workers who preferred not to pay dues, are better off because the bill died without a vote; unions and their members gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent, and no Republican signed on [S4], so the bill never had a path to a floor vote in a Republican-controlled Senate.

industries.note: Unions could require every worker covered by their contract to join or pay dues, expanding membership and revenue. Stronger union finances generally translate into higher pay and better conditions for the workers the union represents.

Employers in right-to-work states would face unions with full membership and dues funding, strengthening labor's side of negotiations. Business groups have long fought right-to-work repeal for this reason.
Workers who do not want to belong to a union could no longer rely on state right-to-work protections and would have to pay dues or fees as a condition of employment.
